Money in the pockets of the poorest households is spent immediately and locally. It supports the shops and businesses in our high streets. Taking it away, or allowing inflation to take it away while standing idle, depresses demand in exactly the communities that can least afford it. My constituents are not asking for luxury; they are asking to be able to keep the lights on, feed their children and get to work. For that reason, we have deliberately designed the framework so that duties are clear, timelines are specified and guidance will be issued well in advance of commencement. Public bodies will not be left guessing about what is expected of them. My Department will publish detailed guidance setting out the practical steps that authorities must take, and we will engage directly with the sectors most affected to ensure that implementation is smooth and consistent across the board. I want to address a concern that has been raised by several Members during the passage of this legislation, namely that some smaller authorities may lack the capacity to comply. I take that concern seriously. That is why we have built in a phased commencement, allowing bodies with fewer resources additional time to put the necessary systems in place, and why funding has been identified to support training and administrative preparation. Compliance should not be a burden borne unequally. Let me also be clear about what this regime is for. It exists to protect beneficiaries — real people whose entitlements and interests depend on public authorities doing their job properly and transparently. Every duty in this Bill traces back to that purpose. Where an authority falls short, beneficiaries and their representatives will have clear routes to raise the matter, first through the complaints mechanisms we are establishing and ultimately, if necessary, through the courts. But I say again that I do not expect litigation to be the norm. The experience of comparable regimes, both in this jurisdiction and elsewhere, is that clear statutory duties, properly communicated, produce high compliance without the need for enforcement action. I am confident that the same will be true here. I commend the provisions to the House and I look forward to working with Members on all sides as we move to implementation.

When a red alert is declared, workers and employers alike should know exactly where they stand: whether the workplace should close, whether staff are entitled to stay home without loss of pay, and what recourse a worker has if an employer insists otherwise. Other countries manage this. They have statutory frameworks for severe weather that remove the ambiguity, and there is no reason we cannot do the same. I am asking the Minister today to commit to bringing forward such a framework — to sit down with the unions and the employer bodies, agree a protocol for status red events, and give it legal effect. What is needed is action on the scale of the emergency: a serious programme of public housing on public land, real protections for renters against unaffordable increases and unjust evictions, and a ban on the practices that allow investment funds to outbid families for the homes being built. The technology to identify and remove this material exists. These are companies that can serve a personalised advertisement to a user within milliseconds of a page loading; the claim that they cannot detect and take down harmful content with comparable speed simply does not withstand scrutiny. What has been lacking is not capability but incentive. As long as the commercial consequences of inaction are negligible, some platforms will continue to treat content moderation as a cost to be minimised rather than a duty to be discharged. That is why the framework we ultimately construct — whether through voluntary undertakings or through statute — must change the incentives. There must be clear expectations about the speed of removal, transparency about how decisions are made, and meaningful consequences when platforms fall short. I would add that this cannot be a matter for the largest companies alone. Experience shows that when material is removed from the major platforms it migrates to smaller ones, and any regime that ignores the long tail of the internet will simply displace the problem rather than solve it. I also want to acknowledge the work of the moderators themselves, often overlooked in these debates — people who view deeply distressing material day after day so that the rest of us do not have to, frequently with inadequate support. Any settlement we reach with the industry should include proper standards for their welfare. The Select Committee's inquiry is asking the right questions, and I look forward to its conclusions. My message to the companies is simple: act now, act quickly and act comprehensively, because if you do not, this House will act for you.

dogs are slaughtered every year for their meat, many of them in conditions of appalling cruelty. They are crammed into cages, transported for days without food or water, and killed by methods that no civilised society could defend. Some are strays; a great many are stolen pets, taken from families who loved them. This trade causes immense suffering, and the United Kingdom, as a nation of dog lovers, should be unambiguous in its opposition to it. Some Members may ask why we need this Bill at all, given that there is no evidence of a widespread practice of dog meat consumption in this country. The answer is twofold. First, there is a genuine legal gap. It is an offence to sell dog meat commercially, but the consumption of dog meat, and its possession for that purpose, is not itself prohibited. That gap should be closed, not because we expect frequent prosecutions, but because the law should state clearly what our values are. Second, and just as important, is the question of international leadership. When the United States Congress passed its prohibition, campaigners across Asia told us that it strengthened their hand in pressing their own governments to act. Countries including Taiwan have already legislated. Every time a Western nation closes this gap in its own law, the argument that this is mere cultural criticism from countries that permit the same practice at home is taken away. This Bill is short, its purpose is simple, and I believe it commands support across the House and across the country. It asks us to say, plainly and in statute, that dogs are companions, not food, and that Britain stands with those around the world campaigning to end this cruel trade. I commend the Bill to the House.

The truth is that this country has, for too long, been a soft touch for dirty money. Our openness — the strength of our financial services, the respect commanded by our courts, the ease of doing business here — has been turned against us by kleptocrats, fraudsters and their professional enablers. We have world-leading laws in some respects, but laws without enforcement are a façade, and the agencies charged with enforcement have been starved of the resources they need. The National Crime Agency's budget is a fraction of the sums laundered through London in a single year. Companies House, until very recently, would register a company to anyone with a few pounds and a plausible name, verifying nothing. The reforms now in train are welcome, and I acknowledge them, but they are the beginning of a task, not its completion. I want to highlight in particular the role of the enablers: the lawyers, accountants and company formation agents without whom none of this would be possible. A shell company does not create itself. The supervisory regime for these professions is fragmented and, in parts, plainly inadequate, and until we consolidate it and give it teeth, we are leaving the door propped open. I also want to echo what has been said about economic crime as a national security issue, not merely a financial one. The events of recent years have shown us where tolerated corruption leads. So I say to the Minister: fund the agencies properly, reform supervision of the enablers, and bring forward the further legislation that everyone in this Chamber knows is needed. The consensus exists. What is required now is urgency.

I want to explain to the House why these changes matter. They are procedural, yes, but procedure is not trivia; procedure is how this place spends its most limited resource, which is time. Under our current practice, hours of sitting time each week are consumed by the mechanics of voting — by bells, by whips gathering members, by votes conducted one after another on questions whose outcomes are not in doubt. Every one of those hours is an hour not spent debating legislation, scrutinising spending or holding the government to account. The proposal before the House does not diminish any member's rights. Any recognized party can still require a recorded vote on any question, and every member's position will still be recorded and published for constituents to see. What it removes is the empty ritual in cases where the result is conceded by all sides. Other parliaments in the Westminster tradition have adopted similar reforms and none has reversed them, because members quickly discover that the time recovered is put to far better use. I acknowledge the concerns raised by some colleagues that streamlined procedures can, over time, tilt the balance toward the government of the day. That concern deserves an answer, and the answer is in the safeguards: the threshold for demanding a recorded division is deliberately low, and the opposition parties retain every tool of delay and protest that they possess today. What we are proposing is not a limit on dissent; it is an end to wasting time when there is no dissent. I urge all members to support the motion.

It means accredited, funded postgraduate pathways for those taking up positions in special classes and special schools, with time allocated to complete them — not evenings and weekends on top of a full teaching load. And it means ongoing access to specialists: speech and language therapists, occupational therapists and psychologists who can work alongside teachers rather than existing at the end of a long waiting list. The number of special classes has grown rapidly, and I welcome that growth, but capacity on paper is not capacity in practice. If we match the expansion of places with an equally serious investment in the people who staff them, we will have something genuinely worth celebrating. I ask the Minister to set out a timeline for exactly that.

Many Russians have shown extraordinary courage in opposing this war — protesters who know they face arrest, journalists who have lost their livelihoods and in some cases their liberty, ordinary citizens who have simply refused to repeat the official lies. History teaches us that regimes of this kind depend on convincing their people that the outside world hates them, that they are encircled, that there is no alternative to the strongman. We should refuse to play the part written for us in that script. That means keeping channels of communication open to Russian civil society wherever we can. It means supporting independent Russian-language media, so that those who want the truth can find it. It means being generous, not grudging, to those Russians who flee persecution for opposing the war — the dissidents, the journalists, the young people who refuse to be conscripted into an unjust invasion. And it means saying plainly that when this war ends, and when Russia has a government that respects its neighbours and its own citizens, there is a path back to normal relations with Europe. A permanent posture of enmity toward the Russian people serves no one except Putin himself. None of this softens our resolve on sanctions, on support for Ukraine, or on the isolation of the regime — those must continue and intensify for as long as the aggression continues. But the measure of our statecraft will be whether we can be hard on the regime while keeping faith with the people it holds hostage. If we manage that, we lay the foundations for a safer Europe. If we fail, we hand the Kremlin its most useful propaganda for a generation.

The ministerial code is a matter for the Prime Minister, who is responsible for its enforcement, and it would not be right for the Chair to insert itself into that process, however strongly the hon. Gentleman feels about the matter — and I appreciate that he feels strongly. What I can say to him, and to the House more widely, is this: there are avenues available to Members who believe that standards have not been upheld. Questions can be tabled, urgent questions can be sought, and the hon. Gentleman is a sufficiently experienced parliamentarian to know how to pursue each of those routes, as he has amply demonstrated this afternoon. If Ministers have made statements to this House that require correction, the position is clear and long established: it is the responsibility of the Minister concerned to correct the record at the earliest opportunity. That expectation is not optional and it does not lapse with the passage of time. The Treasury Bench will have heard the exchange, and I trust that what has been said will be relayed to the Minister in question. Members on both sides of the House should be in no doubt about the seriousness with which the Chair regards accuracy in what is said from the despatch box. The authority of this place rests on the reliability of the information given to it; that is not a partisan point but a constitutional one. As for the hon. Gentleman's wider dissatisfaction, he has put his concerns on the record with his customary force, and they will have been heard by those whose business it is to respond to them. I do not think the matter can usefully be taken further by the Chair today, but he is nothing if not persistent, and I dare say we shall return to these matters before long. We come now to the main business.

It cannot be right that fans who have followed their club for decades, through relegations and rainy Tuesday nights, find themselves priced out or shut out by arrangements made over their heads and without their consent. Football clubs are not ordinary businesses. They are civic institutions, woven into the identity of the towns and cities that sustain them, and any arrangement that treats supporters as an afterthought misunderstands what the game is for. The hon. Member asks what the Government intend to do, and I will tell him. We have made clear to the football authorities that we expect them to resolve this, and to resolve it quickly. The FA, the leagues and the clubs themselves all have levers they can pull, and the strong preference of everyone should be a solution delivered by the game itself rather than imposed from outside. But I say this plainly: if the authorities will not act, the Government retain options, and we are prepared to consider them. The fan-led review has given us a blueprint for the governance of the game, including an independent regulator, and cases such as the one the hon. Member raises strengthen rather than weaken the argument for proceeding with it. In the meantime, my officials are in contact with the parties involved, and I am happy to meet the hon. Member, together with supporter representatives from his constituency, to hear directly from those affected. Weekends like the last one show football at its best — a game with the reach and the standing to change how the nation talks about mental health. The custodians of the game should ask themselves whether arrangements like this one live up to that standing. I do not believe they do, and I suspect that, in their hearts, neither do they.

I want the committee to dwell on that for a moment, because it goes to the heart of how the State procures major projects. If a contractor can win a public tender with a price it does not intend to honour, and then recover the difference through the claims process, then the tender competition is a fiction. The compliant bidders — the ones who priced the job honestly — are punished for their honesty, and the taxpayer pays the difference anyway, just later and with legal costs on top. That is the pattern we have seen not once but repeatedly across major public contracts, and the witnesses before us today have not been able to point to a single structural change that would prevent it happening again. So my questions are these. First, when the tenders were being evaluated, what assessment was made of whether the winning bid was abnormally low? The directives allow — indeed encourage — contracting authorities to interrogate bids that look too good to be true. Was that done, and if so, what did it find? Second, what provision did the contract contain to cap or share the risk of overruns, and why did it fail? And third, what consequence, if any, has there been for the contractor? Has its conduct on this project been taken into account in any subsequent public tender, or has it simply moved on to the next contract with a clean sheet? Because if the answer to that last question is what I suspect it is, then we are not running a procurement system at all. We are running an invitation to underbid.

It is the product of decisions that his party, when it sat on this side of the House, never had the courage to take. I remember the years when Canadians paid among the highest wireless prices in the developed world while the government of the day mused about competition and did precisely nothing. Now, is the job finished? No. Concentration in this sector remains a concern, and I have instructed officials to keep every tool on the table, including spectrum set-asides for regional competitors and stronger mandates for the CRTC. The centre stands today because of her. She never sought recognition and was genuinely embarrassed when it found her. What she sought was simply to be useful, and she was useful to more people than she ever knew. Madeleine passed away last month at the age of 89, surrounded by her family. She leaves her children, her grandchildren and great-grandchildren, and a community that is better in a hundred quiet ways because she lived in it. The lesson of the last two decades in that region is surely that pressure without a credible diplomatic offer produces escalation, while diplomacy without pressure produces empty process. We need both, held together in a single strategy, and I would press the Minister to say more about what that strategy actually is. The joint comprehensive plan of action was imperfect — its critics were right that it did not address ballistic missiles or regional behaviour — but it did verifiably constrain the nuclear programme, and since its collapse the programme has advanced further and faster than at any point in its history. That is the record, and it should chasten anyone who believes that walking away from agreements produces better ones. So when the E3 sit down with our partners, the questions are practical. What is the realistic scope of an agreement that can be reached now, given how far enrichment has proceeded? What sequencing of sanctions relief and nuclear constraints is on the table? And crucially, what channels exist for addressing the regional file — the militias, the missile transfers, the attacks on shipping — in parallel rather than as a precondition, because making everything a precondition of anything is a formula for achieving nothing. I would also urge the Government not to neglect the human dimension. There are dual nationals detained on baseless charges whose families sit in the gallery of our public life waiting for news. Their cases must be raised at every meeting, at every level, without exception. Some of the most harmful content and conduct online is not found on the largest platforms, which — whatever their failings — have at least built moderation systems, trust and safety teams and reporting mechanisms. It is found on small platforms that are small precisely because of what they host: forums dedicated to encouraging suicide and self-harm, sites that organise harassment campaigns, spaces where extremist material circulates freely because moderation is not weak but absent by design. Under the Bill as drafted, those services would face the lightest obligations, while a knitting forum with a large membership could face heavier ones. That cannot be what the Government intend. I understand the counter-argument: that drawing thousands of small services into the full regime would be disproportionate and unworkable, and that the regulator's resources should be focused where the audience is. But that is exactly why a risk-based trigger is the right answer. It would leave the ordinary long tail of the internet untouched, while giving the regulator the power to designate a small service into a higher category where there is evidence of significant risk of serious harm. The regulator would need to justify each designation, the threshold could be set high, and the affected services would have a right of appeal. This is not a novel concept; it is how proportionate regulation works in other sectors, where a small operator handling dangerous material faces obligations a large operator handling safe material does not. The families who have campaigned for this Bill, some of whom have lost children to content hosted on precisely these small platforms, deserve a framework that follows the harm. Federal multiculturalism policy operates in areas of federal jurisdiction, and the notion that it somehow imperils the French language or Quebec's distinct culture has never been supported by evidence; Quebec's culture is vibrant precisely because it has drawn strength from those who have chosen to build their lives in French in North America. Either the true reasons could not be stated, because stating them would have revealed an improper purpose, or those advising decided that the risk of cross-examination outweighed the benefit of candour. Neither possibility reflects well on the Government, and neither is consistent with the duty of candour that the Crown owes to the courts — a duty that is not a technicality but one of the ways in which we distinguish government under law from mere rule. The missing witness, like the dog that did not bark, tells us a great deal. The House should not let the silence pass unremarked.

That practice does heroic work, but no amount of heroism can stretch one surgery across a patient list of that size, and my constituents are living with the consequences: waits of two and three weeks for a routine appointment, phone lines that are engaged solid from 8 am, and older residents who have simply given up trying and present instead at A&E — at many times the cost to the NHS and at real risk to themselves. The pattern my hon. Friend describes and the pattern in Melton are the same, and they share a cause: funding formulas and workforce planning that systematically understate rural need. The formulas reward population density; they do not adequately weigh age — and our populations are older than the national average — nor distance, nor the impossibility of walk-in alternatives that urban patients take for granted. When a practice in a market town loses a partner, there is no neighbouring surgery half a mile away to absorb the list; there is a car journey of many miles, which for an elderly person without transport might as well be a hundred. Meanwhile, housing growth is approved — thousands of new homes across my constituency, which I welcome — but the infrastructure contributions rarely translate into actual additional GP capacity before the residents arrive. The homes come first, the pressure follows immediately, and the health provision limps years behind. So I would ask the Minister, when she responds, to address three things: whether the funding formula review will explicitly weight rurality and age; how the additional roles and training places being created will be steered towards under-doctored rural areas rather than accumulating where recruitment is already easiest; and what mechanism will ensure that large housing developments cannot proceed without commensurate primary care capacity, funded and staffed, not merely promised in a planning document. Our constituents are not asking for special treatment — only for the same access to a family doctor that the rest of the country expects.

A system that treats inconsistency as proof of dishonesty will fail exactly the people it was built for, and hand the traffickers their most useful threat: go to the authorities and they will not believe you. So when we tighten thresholds and timescales, as the measures before us do, we must be honest about who bears the risk of error. If the screening errs against a fraudulent claimant, the system has worked. If it errs against a genuine victim, we return a human being to their exploiters, and no subsequent appeal is much use to someone who has disappeared back into that world. That is why I am asking the Minister for specific safeguards: proper training for first responders, published data on decision outcomes so we can see whether genuine victims are being screened out, and independent review of the new thresholds after twelve months. Get this balance right and we protect both the border and the victim. Get it wrong and we will have traded our proudest recent legislative achievement for a headline, and the people who will pay are those with no voice in this Chamber at all.

That distinction — between the impacts we must now adapt to and the impacts we must at all costs avoid — should be the organizing principle of everything we do in this area, and I want to spell out what it means in practice. On adaptation, it means being honest with communities. There are homes that will flood again. There are coastal roads and rail lines that will have to be moved, not defended. There are farming regions whose growing seasons are changing permanently. Pretending otherwise wastes money on defending the indefensible and, worse, it wastes time that communities need to plan. Adaptation done well is not defeatism; it is the difference between an orderly adjustment and a series of disasters, and it requires funding on a scale we have not yet been willing to commit — because every dollar spent on resilience before a disaster saves several times that in recovery afterwards. That arithmetic is not in dispute; only our willingness to act on it is. But — and this is the crucial point — adaptation has limits, and those limits are exactly the thresholds I have described. You cannot adapt to runaway warming. You cannot build a seawall against the loss of the systems that make agriculture possible. Anyone who presents adaptation as an alternative to emissions reduction is selling a comfort that the science does not permit. The two are not rivals for the same budget; they are the two halves of the only coherent policy, and the balance between them is set by a simple rule: mitigate what you cannot adapt to, adapt to what you can no longer prevent. What is baked in demands our preparation. What is not yet baked in demands our urgency. This decade decides how much falls into each category, and that is why the measures before us matter.

So the contribution will rise on both counts, and the House should be clear about the distinction between the two. One part is automatic: as our economy grows — and it is growing faster than almost any other in the Union — our share of the overall budget rises with it, because contributions are calculated principally by reference to national income. That is not a concession; it is arithmetic, and it reflects something we should acknowledge more often in this House, which is that Ireland has moved from being a substantial net beneficiary of the Union to being a net contributor. I regard that as a mark of success, not a grievance. The generations before us built this country partly with European structural funds — the roads, the training schemes, the rural development programmes that transformed our prospects — and it is right that, having prospered, we now help to fund the same transformation in the newer member states. The second part is the voluntary element I described: a willingness to contribute additional resources in the context of the negotiations now under way, provided — and this is the condition that matters — that the overall package reflects Ireland's priorities. Those priorities are clear: the protection of the Common Agricultural Policy, on which our rural economy depends and which faces pressure in every budget round; continued funding for the programmes that support peace and cross-border cooperation on this island, whose value hardly needs stating in this House; and research and education programmes in which our institutions have performed strongly. Membership of the Union has been the best strategic decision this State ever made, and the sums involved in our contribution are modest against what membership underpins: our access to the single market, our voice at the table, our place in the world. I make no apology for approaching these negotiations constructively, and I believe the vast majority of Irish people would expect nothing less.

The purpose of these provisions is very practical: to ensure that a parent who is owed maintenance for their children can rely on it being paid, regardless of which side of a border — or which court — the original decision came from. Maintenance is not an abstract legal obligation; it is school shoes, heating, the weekly shop. When payment fails, it is children who go without, and any weakening of enforcement is ultimately borne by them. The Lords amendment proceeds from an honourable concern about proportionality, and I acknowledge the spirit in which it was moved. But its effect would be to create two classes of maintenance decision — those enforced with the full toolkit and those enforced with part of it — depending on distinctions that have nothing to do with the needs of the child concerned. A parent in Belfast whose former partner moves abroad would face weaker enforcement than a parent in the identical situation whose former partner remains; that is not proportionality, it is a lottery, and the paying parent most inclined to evade obligations is precisely the one best placed to exploit it. I would also remind the House that the safeguards the Lords sought are already present in the framework: enforcement action is subject to court oversight at every material stage, means are taken into account, and genuine inability to pay is treated entirely differently from refusal to pay. The regime pursues the wilful defaulter, not the struggling one — that distinction is built into its architecture. For those reasons, I ask the House to disagree with the amendment, and in doing so to send a clear message that a child's right to support does not thin out at a border.

That is not incidental context; it is the entire reason the section exists. Section 21 is not a technicality. It embodies the simplest rule in public life: when your private connections and your public duties meet, you step out of the room. Every municipal councillor in this country understands that rule. The committee reports we are debating found that the Prime Minister — the person whose office sets the ethical standard for everyone else in government — did not follow it, and the response from the government benches has been, in essence, that it was all a misunderstanding among friends. But the Commissioner examined that defence directly. The report found that the friendship in question could not reasonably be characterized as the kind of close, continuous personal relationship that the exception contemplates — the contact had been negligible for decades until the member of the family in question was in a position of power. Canadians understand exactly what that pattern is, because they have seen it before: access follows office. So the question before the House is not whether we like the Prime Minister, and it is not about one vacation. It is whether the findings of an independent officer of Parliament carry consequences, or whether accountability in this country now ends at an apology delivered with practiced sincerity. If a report finding multiple contraventions of the Conflict of Interest Act by the head of government produces nothing — no sanction, no restitution, not even a fulsome acknowledgment of the specific findings — then we are teaching every future officeholder that the Act is advisory for the powerful. The records themselves must be preserved, centralised and opened to survivors seeking their own histories; a person's knowledge of their own life must never again depend on an institution's discretion. And the orders that ran these institutions, and that hold assets today, must contribute in proportion to their role — through negotiation if possible, through legislation if not. If cash tips sit outside the redress mechanism, we will have legislated for the tips that were least at risk and left unprotected the tips that were most at risk. I understand the counter-argument about enforceability — that the WRC cannot adjudicate what cannot be evidenced. But other obligations under employment law apply to cash transactions and are enforced through records requirements, and the same route is available here: an obligation to record cash tips received and distributed, with the record open to inspection and to the worker. The obligation itself changes behaviour, even before any complaint is made. I also ask the Minister to look again at the treatment of service charges, because the public believe, reasonably, that a mandatory service charge goes to staff, and anything short of a full guarantee of that in law leaves a deception at the heart of every bill that carries one. First, multi-annual funding for committees, however modest, so they can plan beyond a single season. But I make the comparison for a serious purpose, because the office of Leader of the Opposition matters to this House regardless of who holds it, and the debate we are having today keeps sliding between the officeholder and the office in a way that muddies both. The office deserves respect: it is a constitutional function, not a courtesy title, and the robust scrutiny it exists to provide is part of how this place works. Officeholders, by contrast, earn their standing by how they discharge the function — and it is entirely legitimate for Members on this side to point out when the function is being discharged poorly, just as it was legitimate when the roles were reversed and the barbs flew in the other direction. Those with longer memories than mine assure me the arrows were no blunter then. So let me address the substance beneath the theatre. The shadow Minister's charge was that the Government have treated the Opposition's proposals with contempt. I have checked the record, and it shows the opposite: of the amendments tabled in Committee, the Government accepted several outright and brought forward its own drafting to meet the purpose of others — a fact the shadow Minister omitted, I am sure through inadvertence rather than design. Where we have declined amendments, we have said why, in terms the House can evaluate. That is not contempt; it is the ordinary business of disagreement, conducted in the ordinary way. What would genuinely diminish this place is the habit — growing on both sides, I accept — of treating every rejection as an insult and every disagreement as bad faith. The public watch these exchanges, and they can tell the difference between opposition and grievance. I am confident the Leader of the Opposition needs no defending by me, and, that settled, perhaps we can return to the Bill.

That role was not given to us; it was built, by generations of Irish diplomats, by the Defence Forces personnel who have served on peacekeeping missions without interruption for more than sixty years, and by a consistency of principle that other countries have come to rely upon. When Ireland speaks at the United Nations on disarmament, on hunger, on the rights of small nations, we are listened to beyond our size because our record matches our rhetoric. That is what is at stake in this discussion, and it is why I urge the House to be careful with it. There are voices — the Deputy has heard them as I have — who present our tradition as naivety, as a luxury of an earlier era that a dangerous world can no longer afford. I would argue precisely the opposite: it is in a dangerous world that the honest broker matters most. When the great powers cannot speak to each other, someone must be able to speak to both. When a peace must be monitored, someone must be trusted by both sides to monitor it. The blue helmet on an Irish soldier is respected in south Lebanon and beyond because everyone knows what it does and does not represent. None of this requires us to be silent on aggression — our tradition is neutrality between military blocs, not neutrality between right and wrong, and our record at the United Nations demonstrates that distinction again and again. But it does require us to protect the credibility that makes our voice effective: to resource our peacekeeping commitments properly, to keep our development aid on its path to the UN target, and to ensure that any evolution in our defence arrangements is debated openly with the Irish people, whose instinct on this matter has been sound for seventy years.

So let me offer the House a perspective grounded in that experience rather than in slogans from either direction. The men and women working in the North sea are not the enemies of the energy transition; they are its single greatest asset. The skills that drill and complete a well, that operate and maintain offshore platforms in some of the harshest waters on earth, that manage subsea engineering of extraordinary complexity — these are precisely the skills that offshore wind, carbon capture and hydrogen will need at scale. A country that lets those skills scatter, through a disorderly rundown of the basin, will find itself importing the workforce for its own transition a decade later. That is why I part company with those who talk as though the industry could simply be switched off on a date certain. Demand for oil and gas will continue through the transition — every credible scenario says so — and the only question is whether we meet that demand from our own basin, with among the most regulated production anywhere, supporting our own jobs and our own balance of payments, or whether we import it at higher emissions from regimes that share none of our standards. Importing what we could produce is not climate policy; it is exporting employment while feeling virtuous about it. But I say to my own side, equally: the industry's future depends on earning the transition, not resisting it — on delivering electrification of platforms, on real investment in carbon capture, on the transferability of its people. The sector deal points in that direction. What the workforce needs from this House is neither cheerleading nor condemnation, but a stable, honest framework that keeps the skills together while the destination changes. That is what I will be supporting.

We heard about children taken from their families and returned, if they returned at all, as strangers to their own languages and their own parents. The commission listened, documented and distilled all of that testimony into 94 calls to action — a roadmap written in the words of survivors themselves. And my critique of today's debate is that we speak as though the task before us were still to understand the problem, when the survivors finished explaining it to us years ago. What remains is not comprehension; it is implementation, and the record of implementation is not one any member of this House should be comfortable defending. Count the calls to action fully realized and the number is a fraction of the whole. Child welfare, the very first call, remains in crisis: there are more Indigenous children in care today than at the height of the residential school system. The gaps in funding for education and health that the commission documented persist and are litigated rather than closed. Families are still searching the grounds of former schools for their children, and the supports promised for that heartbreaking work arrive slowly and expire quickly. Meanwhile, every September we gather for commemoration, and commemoration matters — but survivors have told us, repeatedly and plainly, that they did not relive their childhoods before the commission so that Canada could improve its ceremonies. They did it so the country would change. So I say to the government, and truthfully to every party in this House, mine included: pick up the document. Table an implementation schedule with dates and dollars, report against it annually in this chamber, and let the ones who mark the progress be the survivors and their communities, not the departments marking their own work. Reconciliation is not a feeling. It is a debt, it is overdue, and this House holds the ledger.
